newsitem.title: USA: US inventory bulge may help keep Fed policy steady.
newsitem.headline: US inventory bulge may help keep Fed policy steady.

text.p: A recent surge in inventories is likely to have a temporary restraining effect on the U.S. economy, which may prompt the Federal Reserve to keep interest rates steady until November, experts said.

Hardly anyone on Wall Street expects the central bank, captained by chairman Alan Greenspan, to alter the course of monetary policy at the next meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) on Tuesday.
"I would be very surprised, even shocked, if the Fed did anything at this meeting," Lyle Gramley, a former member of the Fed Board of governors, told Reuters.
Gramley said that although the economy remained brisk, the current inventory overhang was likely to pour cold water on an otherwise boiling-hot economic scenario.
"The economy is basically still very, very healthy. But we do have a problem in the inventory area.

"The flow of goods in the inventory is much too large to be sustainable. So that will have to come down, and in the process it will have some degree of a dampening effect on economic growth," Gramley said.
Latest data by the Commerce Department showed June business inventories rose 0.7 percent to $1,025 billion from $1,019 billion in May, and against a $992.1 billion figure a year before.

Analysts said, however, that swelling inventories were not expected to last too long, mainly after recent data showed U.S. consumers appeared to be embarking on a new spending spree in the third quarter after a three-month hiatus.

"The real key here is the pace of final demand because if it's strong enough to draw down those inventories, you will come out of this situation with still a healthy economy," said Richard Berner, chief economist at Mellon Bank Corp.

In a recent report, a Salomon Brothers research team said the pickup in demand against the backdrop of stepped-up business inventory investment was likely to boost Gross Domestic Product growth to between 3.0 and 4.0 percent over the remainder of the year.

"The eventual confirmation that the economy has resumed its above-trend trajectory should prompt further tightening in monetary policy and intermittent upward pressure on (Treasury) bond yields later this year," the report said.
Trend growth for the U.S. economy is perceived by the market to be somewhere between 2.0 and 2.5 percent.
Most analysts expected the Fed to fine-tune monetary policy later in 1997 with another interest rate hike in an effort to avert any inflationary threat that may arise.

Wall Street's current preferred date for a next raise in interest rates is the Fed's FOMC meeting on November 12. The Fed last changed monetary policy on March 25, when it lifted the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent.
"I think there's a 50/50 chance they'll act in November. But I wouldn't think they would act before that," said Gramley, who is now a consulting economist for the Mortgage Bankers Association.

Elsewhere in the economy, analysts said a lack of growth in the civilian labor force for four straight months was likely, if maintained, to put extra downward pressure on the jobless rate and, eventually, become a source of concern for the Fed.
The unemployment rate is currently at 4.8 percent, a near quarter-century low.

Among other indicators the Fed was likely to be looking at during Tuesday's FOMC meeting, analysts pointed to a neutral 4.7 percent year-over-year growth in M2 and a strong 8.3 percent rise on year-over-year total bank loans.
Analysts said the real fed funds rate -- the nominal rate less the variation of inflation -- was currently around 3.1 percent, which is mostly seen as neutral to mildly restrictive.
